title: [Volcanic chains of Japan]
caption_extra: Volcanic Chains. According to the Geological Research Office, the total number of volcanoes in Japan is 192, of which 58 are active. They may be grouped in 11 chains:

rows: The north Japan inner, or Chokai, volcanic chain, which starts at the south-western offing of Hokkaido, or O-shima and Ko-jima, and runs through Iwaki-yama, Kampuzan, Moriyoshi-yama Chokai-san, ending with Gassan.

The south Japan inner, or Hakusan, volcanic chain, extending from Hakusan along the Japan Sea to the west through Daisen, Mitsubé-yama, Aono-yama and other smaller volcanoes and then to the Goto Islands of Kyushu.
The Hokkaido volcanic chain, which links such mountains as Hakodaté-yama, Komaga-daké, Tarumayé-daké and some islands in the peninsular part of western Hokkaido.

The north Japan central, or Nasu, volcanic chain, including Osoré-yama, Hakkoda-san, Towada Lake, Iwaté-yama, Komaga-daké, Kurigoma, Numasawa, Arao, Funagata, Za-oh, Bantai, Azuma, Adatara, Nasu, Nantai, Shirané, Akagi, Haruna, Tsuno-otoshi and Arafuna, which are mostly active volcanoes.
The Hida volcanic chain, composed of the seven volcanoes of Hera-daké, Taté-yama, Ko-tombi, Washiba-daké, Iwo-daké, Norikura-daké and On-také.

The Mikasa volcanic chain, to the west of the Hida volcanic chain, beginning with Horaiji-san, of Aichi prefecture, and running westward to O-hara-yama, Mikasa-yama, Miminari-yama, Futakami-san and Kabuto-yama of Hyogo prefecture.

The Seto, or Inland Sea, volcanic chain, embracing the old volcanic mountains along the coasts of the Inland Sea and extending to Kyushu, including such mountains as Futako, Kokonoyé, Yufu, Onsen and Tara. The volcanoes are all dormant.

The Ryukyu volcanic chain, starting with the Aso volcano, taking in Kirishima, Sakurajima and Kaimon and extending to the Ryukyu Islands, where it connects Iwojima, Kuchino-Irabé-jima, Kuchinosé, Nakano-jima, Suwanosé, Waruiwa-jima, Tori-shima and Aguni-shima.

The amphibolite andesite volcanic chain, which connects Aono-yama of Shimané prefecture and Tokusa of Yamaguchi, appears then in Kimpo-zan and Shiguma-daké near Tokuyama, and Himé-jima of Suo, meets with the Inland Sea chain and runs to Yufu, Kokonoé and a part of Aso, and extends as far as Luzon Island, sinking to the bottom of the ocean west of the Ryukyu Islands on the way and then running along the eastern coast of Formosa.

The Fuji volcanic chain, which cuts across the heart of the Main Island from the coast of the Japan Sea to that of the Pacific Ocean, and continues to the Izu, Bonin, Sulphur, Mariana and Caroline Islands, including such mountains as Myoko, Togakushi-yama, Tateshina-yama, Yatsuga-daké, Fuji-san, Hakoné and Amagi on the Main Island.
The Chishima volcanic chain, which comes into Hokkaido from the Chishima, runs along the Ezo mountain system, suddenly turns to the north and seems to disappear in Saghalin.

title: [Buké Shohatto (Samurai Law), 1615: gist of the 13 articles]

rows: Samurai must be well educated in general learning and versed in the arts of war
Unbridled drinking and luxuriousness are strictly prohibited
Criminals must not be aided or concealed
All treasonous bodies and murderers should be banished
No person other than the subjects of the daimyo of a district should be allowed to live in his territory
All repairs to castles need permission of the Shogunate and the building of a new castle is strictly prohibited
If anyone detects a new castle building or a secret political organization in a neighboring province he must report it to the Shogunate
Marriages must not be celebrated privately

All the lords are required to observe “sankin-kotai.” (According to this article the lords were divided into two groups, and each group was to come up to Yédo, the seat of the Shogunate, in April every other year, to stay there for one year and the Shogunate prepared their Yédo residences where their families were kept as hostages. These rules were somewhat loosened in later years)
Styles of costume should be regulated according to rank and social position
Servants ought not freely to use the palanquin (the only vehicle in those days) in travel
Samurai should be instructed to live frugally
the lords should use discretion in appointment of officials

title: [Five articles of the Imperial oath, 14 March 1868]
caption_extra: New Japan — Meiji Era (1868–1912 A.D.) — The Meiji Restoration

rows: We will call councils and rule the nation according to public opinion
Men of upper and lower classes without distinction shall be united in all enterprises
Civil officials and military officers shall be in one accord and all the common people shall be so treated that they can attain their aims and feel no discontent
Old unworthy ways and customs shall be destroyed and the people shall walk along the highway of heaven and earth
Knowledge shall be sought among the nations of the world and the Empire shall be led up to the zenith of prosperity.

footnotes: “To accomplish this unprecedented reformation, We go before the people, and proclaim the fundamental national principles even in the presence of the gods of heaven and earth, to establish the way for the public welfare. Ye, Our subjects, shall be united all together, according to these principles.”

title: Chronicle of Important Historical Events in Japan and the World

parts.label: Japan
rows: Beginning of the Empire (660 B.C.–531 A.D.)
The First Tenno Jimmu ascends the Throne at Kashiwara, in the present Nara prefecture.
The Great Shrine of Isé built by the eleventh Tenno Suinin.
The 9th year of the Tenno Suinin.
Kyushu and the eastern half of the Main Island subdued by the twelfth Tenno Keiko and Prince Yamato-takeru.
The Empire divided for the first time into administrative districts by the thirteenth Tenno Seimu.
Silla conquered by the Empress Jingo.
The sixteenth Tenno Nintoku establishes the capital at Naniwa (Osaka) for the convenience of intercourse with Korea.
The Tenno Nintoku relieves the people by a three year remission of taxes.
Japanese Office in Mimana destroyed by Silla.
Imperial Prince Shotoku, Regent, builds Horyuji and Shitennoji temples.
The Constitution of Seventeen Tables published by the Regent Shotoku.
The first envoy sent to the Sui Court of China.
The first envoy sent to the Tang Court of China.
Control over the Korean peninsula abandoned.
The Taiho Law promulgated and the organization of the Imperial Government fixed.
Nara founded as the capital by the Empress Gemmyo (the forty-third ruler).
The first books of Japanese history, Nihon Shoki (Japanese Annals) and Kojiki (Antiquities) compiled.
The treasures of the Tenno Shomu donated to Todaiji temple by the Empress Komyo, and later building of the Shoso-in Museum for their preservation.
Dictatorship of Dokyo, Buddhist “pope,” opposed by the loyalist Waké-no-Kiyomaro.
Heian (Kyoto) founded as the new capital by the fiftieth Tenno Kammu.
Establishment of governmental and private schools.
Fujiwara-Yoshifusa assumes the Regency. Rise of the Fujiwaras.
Fujiwara-Mototsune, the Daijo Daijin and Regent, appointed the first Kampaku (Chief Councillor to the Throne).
Official intercourse with the Tang Dynasty broken off.
Pohai, a maritime monarchy in Manchuria trades with Japan.
Sugawara-Michizane, candidate for Kampaku, reduced to the governor of Kyushu by the Fujiwara scandal.
Samurai families of Minamoto (Genji) and Taira (Heishi or Heike) gradually rise to power.
Climax of the Fujiwara despotism and prosperity.
Armies of Buddhist monks disturb the capital.
Rise of the Minamotos in rivalry to the Tairas. Minamoto-Yoritomo establishes headquarters at Kamakura.
The Tairas destroyed by the Minamotos. Minamoto-Yoritomo appoints local military police and tax-gatherers.
Minamoto-Yoritomo appointed Seii-Tai-Shogun (Generalissimo) and the Shogun Government formally sanctioned. For the following 675 years Japan ruled by the samurai statesmen.
The Kamakura Shogunate ended with the third Shogun, Minamoto-Sanetomo But Masako, widow of Yoritomo officiates as a nun Shogun for several years.
Hojo-Yasutoki becomes chief executive of the Kamakura Shogunate. The Hojos exercise the Shogun's duties for over a century.
The Joei Code promulgated for the discipline of the samurai.
Second Yuan invasion and defeat by the armies of Hojo-Tokimune, the chief-executive.
An attempt for the restoration of the Imperial rule.
Battles between the Imperial and the Hojo armies.
The Hojos destroyed. Temporary restoration of the Imperial direct rule by the Tenno Godaigo.
Death of Kusunoki-Masashige, loyalist, in the battle of the Minatogawa (Kobe). The Imperial House divided into two, the South and the North (Yoshino and Kyoto) for 57 years.
Ashikaga-Takauji proclaims himself Shogun and establishes the Muromachi Shogunate in Kyoto.
The Onin war. Kyoto reduced to ashes. The Court and the Shogunate both lost power before rising feudal lords.
Importation of copper money from the Ming Dynasty.
Duel between individual prohibited by the Muromachi Shogunate.
Chinese trade boats come to Bungo in Kyushu.
Portuguese trade boats come to Buzen in Kyushu.
Oda-Nobunaga comes up to Kyoto by Imperial order.
Nobunaga destroys Enryakuji temple to suppress the power of Buddhist monks.
Building of the Azuchi castle by Nobunaga.
Unification of the Empire by Hideyoshi.
Battle of Sekigahara assures the supremacy of Tokugawa-Iyeyasu (1542–1616 A.D.)
Iyeyasu appointed Shogun. Founding of the Tokugawa Shogunate in Yedo (Tokyo).
Beginning of the trade with Hollanders. The Loochoo Islands subjugated by Lord Shimazu.
Official letter to Nova-Hispania and Spain.
Hasekura sent to Rome by Lord Date-Masamune.
The Toyotomis destroyed by the Tokugawas at the Battle of Osaka.
Promulgation of the Kuge Shohatto (Court Nobles Law) and the Buke Shohatto (Samurai Law).
Japan closed. Foreign nationals prohibited to enter Japan, except the Hollanders and the Chinese.
The compilation of the Dai Nippon Shi (Great Japanese History) begun by Lord Tokugawa-Mitsukuni completed.
The Genroku Era of ornate living.
The Prohibition Law against Western books amended.
Motoori-Norinaga commences his commentary on the Kojiki (Antiquities).
Establishment of a Governmental medical school.
Private societies or mobs among the peasants forbidden.
Administrative reform by the Roju, Matsudaira-Sadanobu (Rakuo).
Coming of an English boat to Nagasaki.
A map of the coast lines of Japan completed.
Shogunate Order to shut out all foreign ships by force.
Great famine of the Tempo era.
Rebellion of Oshio-Heihachiro to relieve the starving masses.
The 1825 Order removed. A step toward opening the country.
Controversies between the antiforeign party and the liberalists.
Visit of American ships to Uraga.
First request of America for the “open door.”
Casting of a European gun by Sakuma-Shozan.
Knocking at Japan's doors of British and American ships.
Arrival of the American fleet under Commodore Perry.
Visit of the Russian delegate Poutiatine to Nagasaki.
Conclusion of Amity Treaties with the United States, Great Britain and Russia.
Institution of the Sun Flag to symbolize Japan. (Sanctioned by the Government in 1870).
Conclusion of Amity Treaty with Holland.
Arrival of the American envoy Townsend Harris.
Conclusion of Commercial Treaties with the United States, Great Britain, France, Russia and Holland.
The Ansei Coup d'Etat by the Tairo, Ii Kamonnokami (Naosuké).
Ports of Yokohama, Hakodaté and Nagasaki opened.
Japan's envoy Niimi-Masaoki sent to the United States.
The British Legation at Yedo attacked by the ronin.
The Anti-Foreign Law. Attack on foreign ships at Shimonoseki and Kagoshima.
Battle at the Hamaguri gate of the Kyoto Imperial Palace.
Shimonoseki bombarded by a combined fleet of the United States, Great Britain, France and the Netherlands.
Imperial Sanction given to the treaties of 1858.
Hostilities between the Shogunate and Anti-Shogunate forces.
Accession of Meiji Tenno (1852–1912 A.D.), the 122nd Emperor.
Imperial armies moved against the Yedo Shogunate.
Proclamation of the Restoration of Imperial direct rule.
On October 14, the Shogun Yoshinobu Tokugawa petitioned for the return of all authority of the Government to the Throne, and, on the 24th, the petition was accepted.
Formal enthronement of Meiji Tenno. The first year of Meiji, beginning with September, 1868.
The Five Articles of Imperial Oath declared.
Removal of the Capital to Tokyo.
Surrender of fiefs by feudal lords.
The country divided into 81 gubernatorial districts.
The people allowed to cut off their cues and the samurai forbidden to wear swords.
Institution of the national school system.
Opening of the first railway line between Tokyo and Yokohama.
Institution of the conscription system for national defense.
Request for opening the national assembly.
The South-Western Civil War, or rebellion of Saigo-Takamori.
Rapid influx of things and ideas from Europe; Rokumei-kan period.
Promulgation of a new Penal Code.
Imperial Edict for the opening of the national assembly.
Ito-Hirobumi sent to Europe for the study of Western constitutional governments.
Establishment of the Bank of Japan.
Japan becomes a member of the International Red Cross Society.
Proclamation of the Constitution of the Empire of Japan Feb. 11.
The First Session of the Imperial Diet convened in November.
The Imperial Rescript on Education issued.
Institution of the system of law courts.
Russian Crown Prince injured at Otsu.
Three Powers' Intervention and return of the Liaotung Peninsula to China.
“Gentlemen's” Agreement between the United States and Japan.
Revision of Treaties with the United States, Great Britain and other Western countries on equal footing.
Demise of the Tenno Meiji, July 30.
Accession of the Tenno Taisho, July 30.
The South Sea Islands mandated to Japan.
Japan joins the League of Nations.
The Washington Conferences. Ended the Anglo-Japanese Alliance.
Great Earthquake of Kanto district, September 1.
Promulgation of the new Election Law (Universal Suffrage).
Demise of the Tenno Taisho, Dec. 25.
Accession of the present Tenno, Dc. 25.
First general election under the Universal Suffrage Law.
The Shanghai Affair. Independence of Manchuria, declared Mar. 1.
The “May 15 Affair.” Prime Minister Inukai-Tsuyoshi assassinated.
Japan quits the League of Nations, Mar.
The World Economic Conference at London.
Manchuria becomes an Empire with Pu Yi as first Emperor, Mar. 1.
Japanese Government notifies the U.S. Government its intention to terminate the Washington Naval Treaty, Dec. 29.
Japan quits the London Naval Understanding of 1930.
The “February 26 Affair.” Thren political dignitaries assassinated.
The “China Affair,” July 7. Occupation of Shanghai by the Japanese forces, Nov. 10.
The Kuomintang Government removed to Hankow.
Conclusion of the new Japanese-Dutch commercial agreement, Feb. 2.
Japan announces the withdrawal of its cooperation with all committees of the League of Nations, Oct. 3.
Hankow, Wuchang and Hanyang occupied by Japanese forces, Oct. 27.
Japanese Government issues a statement on Japan's future policy for the settlement of the China Affair, Nov. 3.
Cultural agreement between Japan and Germany, Nov. 25.
The China Affairs Board created, Dec. 16.
Konoe Statement regarding the adjustment of the Sino-Japanese relations, Dec. 22.
Change of the Cabinet from Konoe to Hiranuma, Jan. 5.
Hainan Island surprised by the landing of Japanese forces, Feb. 10.
Cultural Agreement between Italy and Japan, March 23.
Blockade of the Foreign Concessions in Tientsin by the Japanese Army, June 14.
Swatow occupied by the Imperial forces, June 21.
Air Battle between Japanese and Soviet war-planes above Lake Buirnor, June 27.
Abrogation of the Japanese-American Commercial Treaty by the United States, July 26.
Trade agreement between Japan and Germany, July 29.
Anglo-Japanese Parley in Tokyo adjourned sine die, Aug. 14.
Japan's policy of non-involvement in European hostilities announced, Sept. 4.
Truce between the Japanese and Russian forces at Nomonhan in Outer Mongolia, Sept. 15.
Treaty of Amity between Japan and Iran, Oct. 18.
The round-the-world flight of the airplane ‘Nihon,’ Oct. 20.
The yen linked to American dollar instead of Sterling, Oct. 25.
Provisional Fishery Agreement between Japan and the U.S.S.R., Dec. 31.
The new cabinet under Admiral Yonai-Mitsumasa installed, Jan. 16.
The M.S. Asama Maru case, Jan. 21.
The expiration of the Japanese-American Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1911, Jan. 26.
The 75th Session of the Imperial Diet reopened, Feb. 1.
Foreign Minister Arita notifies the diplomatic representatives of Germany, the Netherlands, Great Britain and France, of Japan's policy of non-involvement in the war, May 11.
The Treaty of Amity and Mutual Respect of Territories between Japan and Thailand signed at Tokyo, June 12.
The barricades around the foreign concession at Tientsin removed, June 20.
Manufacture and sale of luxury articles prohibited, July 7.
Prince Konoyé reappointed as Premier, July 22.
The Seiyukai Party dissolves after 40 years of its history, July 30.
Japanese troops enter North French Indo-China in accordance with the Japanese-French understanding, Sept. 23.
The Tripartite Alliance among Japan, Germany and Italy signed in Berlin, Sept. 27.
The inaugural meeting of Taisei Yokusan Kai held at the Premier's official residence, Oct. 12.
Celebration commemoration of the 2600th year of the founding of the Empire of Japan, Nov. 10.
Prince Saionji-Kimmochi succumbs at Okitsu, No. 30.
Conclusion of the Treaty concerning the Basic Relations between Japan and Wang Ching-wei's government, Nov. 30.
The 76th Session of the Diet convened. Dec. 24.
Foreign Minister Matsuoka-Yosuke leaves Tokyo on his trip to Germany and Italy, Mar. 12.
Matsuoka meets Hitler in Berlin, Mar. 27.
The primary educational system reformed, Apr. 1.
Foreign Minister Matsuoka and Premier Mussolini confer in Rome, Apr. 1.
Japanese office at Geneva formally closed, Apr. 2.
Signing of the Neutrality Pact between Japan and the U.S.S.R. in Moscow, Apr. 13.
Foreign Minister Matsuoka returns to Tokyo, Apr. 22.

Conclusion of the two pacts between Japan and France, i.e. the Convention of Establishment and Navigation and the Agreement concerning Customs Tariff, Trade and Method of Payment, both relating to economic relations between Japan and French Indo-China, May 6.
The National Defense Security Law enforced, May 10.
The first Central Cooperative Council of the Taisei Yokusan Kai held for 5 days, Juny 16–20.
The economic parley between Japan and the Dutch East Indies breaks up, June 17.
The subterranean Shimonoseki–Moji Kyushu opened, July 10.
The second Konoé Cabinet tenders resignation to the Throne, July 16.
Prince Konoé organizes his third cabinet by the Imperial Order, July 18.
The Joint Defense Protocol between Japan and France concerning the protection of French Indo-China concluded, and Japanese forces landed on Saigon, July 29.
The third Konoé Cabinet resigns en bloc, Oct. 16.
The new Cabinet with General Tojo-Hideki as Prime Minister installed, Oct. 18.
The despatch of Ambassador Kurusu-Saburo to the United States to aid Ambassador Admiral Nomura in the American-Japanese negotiation, Nov. 5.
The 77th session of the Diet convened, Nov. 15.
United States Secretary of State Cordell Hull hands a document concerning the adjustment of the American-Japanese relations to Ambassadors Nomura and Kurusu, Nov. 26.
The Pacific War, Japan declares war against the U.S.A. and Britain, December 8, following her attack on Pearl Harbor.
The British warships Prince of Wales and Repulse sunk by the Japanese Naval Air Forces off the eastern coasts of the Malay Peninsula, Dec. 10.
Commencement of air raids on North Australia, Dec. 11.
The 78th Session of the Diet convoked, Dec. 15.
The Alliance Pact between Japan and Thailand signed at Bangkok, Dec. 21.
Hong Kong, British Crown Colony occupied by the Japanese forces, Dec. 25.
Manila brought under the Japanese Military Administration by the agreement reached between the Japanese Army Headquarters in the Philippines and J.B. Vargas, new Mayor of Manila, Jan. 7.
Singapore falls into the hand of the Japanese Army when British Commander Robert Percival surrenders, Feb. 15.
Batavia occupied by the Japanese Army, Mar. 8.
Java surrenders to the Japanese forces, Mar. 9.
Tokyo and other cities are attacked for the first time by a small number of American warplanes, Apr. 18.
Corregidor is occupied by the Japanese Forces, May 7.
The 80th Session of the Diest convoked, May 25.
General Koiso-Kuniaki appointed Governor-General of Korea in succession to General Minami-Jiro, May 29.
Burma is placed under the Japanese Military Administration, June 4.
Battle between the Japanese Navy and a combined Anglo-American fleet off the Solomon Islands, Aug. 14.
The diplomatic exchange vessels, the Asama Maru and the Conte Verde arrive at Yokohama, Aug. 20.
The second Solomon sea battle, Aug. 24.
The Ministry for the Greater East Asia is established, Nov. 1.
The third Solomon sea battle, Nov. 14.
Japanese Navy planes intensively bomb Port Moresby, Nov. 30.
A Japanese destroyer squadron launches an attack on a naval unit off Lunga on Guadalcanar Island, Nov. 30.
The 81st Session of the Diet convened, Dec. 24.
Abolition of extra-territorial rights of the Japanese in China and retrocession of concessions and international settlements in China by Japan, Jan. 9.
Economic pacts between Japan and Germany, and Japan and Italy signed at Berlin and Rome, Jan. 20.
Battle in waters east of Rennel Island of the Solomons, Jan. 29.
A cultural Agreement between Japan and Bulgaria concluded, Feb. 11.
The Japanese Army and Navy forces enter into Kwangchow Bay, the French leased territory in China, Feb. 21.
Premier Tojo's visit to Nanking, Mar. 12–15.
Ba Maw, Chief of the Administration Council of Burma arrives in Tokyo, Mar. 18.
The fulfilment of Japan's retrocession of concessions and relinquishment of extra-territorial rights in China, Mar. 30.
Premier Tojo's visit to Hsinking, Apr. 1–4.
Premier Tojo's visit to Manila, May 5–8.
The Japanese occupation of Maungdaw, Burma, May 18.
The death of Fleet-Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, Commander-in-Chief of the Combined Fleet, on the southern Pacific front, May 21.
Attu Island occupied by the U.S. forces, May 29.
Japan recognizes the new Argentine Government headed by General P. Ramirez formed on June 7, June 11.
The 82nd Session of the Diet is convened, June 15.
An agreement pertaining to the retrocession to China of the International Settlement of Shanghai signed at Nanking, June 30.
Tokyo is made Tokyo Metropolis with the amalgamation of the prefectural and municipal administrative organs, July 1.
Premier Tojo's visit to Bangkok, July 3–5.
Ohtorishima (former Wake Island) is attacked by the American bombers, July 25.
The declaration of Independence of Burma and the conclusion of Japan-Burma Alliance, Aug. 1.
The Kuriles attacked by an American air unit, Aug. 12.
The complete abandonment of Kiska Island by the Japanese Army and Navy forces, Aug. 22.
The U.S. forces commence landing on New Guinea, Sept. 4.
The “Tei-A Maru” leaves Yokohama for the second exchange of Japanese and American people interned in the respective countries, Sept. 14.
A joint communique of the Japanese and German Governments on the continuous validity of the Tripartite Alliance of Japan, Germany and Italy, Sept. 15.
Recognition by the Japanese Government, Thailand and Manchoukuo of the new Republic of the Philippines, Oct. 15.
The exchange of Japanese and American nationals who were brought to Murmagao by the “Tei-A Maru” and the “Gripsholm” respectively completed, Oct. 19.
Formal recognition by the Japanese Government of the Provisional Government of Azad Hind (Free State of India), Oct. 23.
The conclusion of a Pact between the Japanese Government and the Nanking Government under Wang Ching-wei on Oct. 30.
A five-point joint declaration adopted by the so-called Assembly of Greater East Asiatic Nations, Nov. 6.
Japanese forces of 3,000 garrisoned on Tarawa and Makin Islands of the Gilbert Group make their last charge, Nov. 25.
All the officers and men of the Japanese forces on Kuezyerin and Ruot Islands in the Marshall Group, meet their death, Feb. 6.
Jorge B. Vargas, first Philippine Ambassador to Japan, and his suite arrive in Tokyo, Feb. 10.
General Hideki Tojo, Premier and War Minister, is appointed Chief of the Army General Staff and Admiral Shigetaro Shimada, Navy Minister, Chief of the Navy General Staff, Feb. 21.

Agreements for the transfer of Japanese oil and coal concessions in northern Saghalien to the Soviet Union and for the prolongation for five years of the Fishery Convention between the two countries signed in Moscow, Mar. 30.
Admiral Mine-ichi Koga, commander-in-chief of the Japanese Combined Fleet, dies at his post in March.
More than 10 American planes coming from a Chinese base attack Kyushu, July 8.
Saipan Island occupied by the U.S. forces, July 16.

Emperor commands General Kuniaki Koiso, Governor-General of Korea, and Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai, former Premier, to cooperate in organizing a new cabinet, following the resignation of the Tojo Cabinet, July 20.
The U.S. force of two divisions land on Guam Island, July 21.
The American troops land on Tenian Island, July 23.
80 American planes attack Kyushu and the western part of the Chugoku area, Aug. 20.
American contingents land on Palau Island, Sept. 15.
Mitsuru Toyama, well-known Japanese nationalist, succumbs to illness at the ripe age of ninety, Oct. 4.
The American troops land at Tacloban in Leyte Island in the Philippines, Oct. 20.
Wang Ching-wei of the Nanking Government of China passes away in Nagoya, Nov. 10.
The air-raids by B-29 bombers on the Main Islands of Japan intensify, beginning with the attack on Tokyo area on Nov. 27 (See Chapter on the Pacific War).
About one division of American troops land at San Jose on Mindoro Island, Dec. 15.
American forces that entered Lingayen Bay commence landing at San Fabian and at Lingayen, Jan. 9.
American forces begin landing on Iojima, Feb. 19.
Japanese forces in Iwojima make their last charge, Mar. 17.
Carrier borne planes attack the southern and eastern parts of Kyushu, March 18.
The U.S. forces begin landing on the main island of Okinawa, Apr. 1.
Admiral Baron Kantaro Suzuki, President of the Privy Council, forms a new Cabinet, following the resignation of the Koiso Cabinet, Apr. 5.
American troops land on Iye Island, west of the Okinawa Island, Apr. 20.
American forces start landing at Tarakan Islands in Borneo, Apr 27.
Japanese Foreign Office announces the Tripartite Pact between Japan, Germany and Italy deemed to have ceased to be effective, May 16.
Field-Marshal Prince Kotohito Kan-in succumbs at the age of 81 years, May 20.
About 900 American carrier-borne planes attack air bases in southern Kyushu, May 23.
An American task force bombard Hitachi and Mito, July 16.
About 250 American carrier-planes, fighters and bombers attack Yokosuka Naval Port, July 18.
About 2,000 American planes of Superforts, fighters and carrier planes, carry out raids on various parts of Japan including Osaka, July 24.
About 270 carrier-planes attack Kinki and Kanto districts, July 30.
About 600 superforts attack Tsurumi, Kawasaki, Toyama, Mito, Tachikawa, Hachioji and Nagaoka, Aug. 2.
An atomic bomb attack on Hiroshima, Aug. 6.
An Imperial Rescript issued announcing the end of the war, Aug. 14.
War Minister General Korechika Anami kills himself, Aug. 14.
Suzuki Cabinet resigns en bloc, Aug. 15.
Prince Naruhiko Higashi-kuni forms his Cabinet, Aug. 17.
Advance units of the Allied Occupation Forces arrive at the Atsugi Airfield, Aug. 28.
General Douglas MacArthur, Commander-in-Chief of the Allied Forces, arrives at the Atsugi Airfield, Aug. 30.
Japan signs the instrument of surrenders aboard the Battleship Missouri, Sept. 2.
General Hideki Tojo attempts suicide, Sept. 11.
General MacArthur orders the apprehension of 38 Japanese and foreign war crimes suspects, Sept. 11.
Field-Marshal Gen. Sugiyama and Mrs. Sugiyama commit suicide, Sept. 12.
The Japanese Imperial Headquarters ceases to exist at midnight, Sept. 13.
The control of newspapers and news agencies removed, Sept. 22.
The Emperor calls on General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, at the American Embassy, Sept. 27.
The dissolution of the Domei News Agency, Sept. 30.

A SCAP memorandum is issued ordering 1—the liberation of all political prisoners, 2—the abolition of the secret police, 3—the removal from office of the Home Minister, and 4—the abrogation and immediate suspension of wartime laws, Oct. 4.
The Higashikuni Cabinet resigns en bloc, Oct. 5.
The Emperor expresses desire to revise the Imperial Constitution, Oct. 13.
The dissolution of the secret police of 4,800 members, Oct. 14.
General Douglas MacArthur broadcasts from Tokyo to the U.S.A., Oct. 15.
The issuance of a SCAP directing ordering the immediate dismissal of all militarists and ultra-nationalists from the Japanese educational field, Oct. 31.
A SCAP directive ordering the government to freeze the property of the Imperial Family amounting to ¥1,5000,000,000, Nov. 20.
General Baron Shigeru Honjo commits suicide, Nov. 20.
The demobilization of all servicemen within the Japanese territory completed, Nov. 28.
The arrest of 59 high-ranking Japanese war crimes suspects including Prince Morimasa Nashimoto, Dec. 3.
The apprehension by Dec. 16 of nine additional high-ranking Japanese, including Prince Fumimaro Konoyé, Dec. 6.
General Tomoyuki Yamashita sentenced to death by hanging, Dec. 8.
Prince Fumimaro Konoyé ends his life by taking poison, Dec. 16.
The ending of Japanese government sponsorship and financial support of State Shinto, Dec. 16.
The Emperor renounces his divinity in the Imperial rescript, Jan. 1.
The Far Eastern Commission arrives in Japan, Jan. 9.
Sanzo Nozaka, noted Communist, returns to Tokyo, from Yenan, Jan. 13.
The Shidehara Cabinet completes its reshuffle, Jan. 13.
The public prostitution system of Tokyo is abolished, Jan. 15.
The Japanese government announces the scope of persons to be removed from public services in accordance with the January 4 SCAP directive Feb. 9.
The arrival of the U.S. Education Mission, headed by Dr. George I. Stoddard at Atsughi Airfield, Mar. 5.
The Revised Japanese Constitution Drafted announced by the Japanese government, Mar. 6.
The first shipment to America of Japanese silk (1,100 bales) from Yokohama, Mar. 19.
Lieutenant-General Masaharu Homma, former Supreme Commander of the Japanese Forces to the Philippines shot dead by a firing squad in a suburb of Manila, Apr. 2.
The first meeting of the Allied Council for Japan held at the Meiji Building, Tokyo, Apr. 5.
The report of the United States Education Mission on Japanese education submitted to General Douglas MacArthur, Apr. 7.
The first post-surrender general election in Japan, Apr. 10.
After a decade of oblivion, May Day is celebrated, May 1.
Twenty-eight Class-A war crimines suspects arraigned at the court of the International Tribunal for the Far East, May 3.
The former U.S. President Herbert Hoover arrives at Atsughi airfield from Korea to investigate the food condition in the Far East, May 5.
The arrival of General Dwight Eisenhower, Chief of the U.S. General Staff, in Tokyo, May 10.
Edwin Pawley, President Truman's special envoy on reparations, arrives in Tokyo, May 10.
Foreign Minister Shigeru Yoshida becomes the president of the Liberal Party, May 15.
Shigeru Yoshida, President of the Liberal Party, forms a new Cabinet, May 20.
Yosuke Matsuoka, former Foreign Minister and one of the 28 top-ranking Japanese officials accused as war criminals, dies, June 27.
The immediate abolition of Japan's peerage system with the enforcement of the new Constitution approved by the House of Representatives, Aug. 3.

Pope Pius XII places $20,000 at the disposal of Japanese churches for reconstruction of edifices destroyed during the war. One hundred and two Roman Catholic churches in Japan were destroyed and damaged, Aug. 8.
The resumption of the Antarctic whaling under SCAP permission, Aug. 20.
The U.S. State Department announces that Mrs. Elizabeth Gray Vining, 44, of Philadelphia, has been appointed tutor to Crown Prince Akihito, Aug. 29.
The dissolution of the Butokukai, or the Japan Martial Art Society, Sept. 13.
The dissolution of the big three “Zaibatsu,” the Mitsuis, Mitsubishis and Yasudas, announced by themselves, Sept. 30.
The Labour Relations Readjusttment Bill, previously adopted at the Diet goes into effect, Oct. 13.
The promulgation of the new Constitution, Nov. 3.
The Ministry of Education makes public a list of the Chinese ideographs recognised for current use, 1,850 in number, Nov. 6.

SCAP orders the Japanese Government to convert the whole assets of the ten big Zaibatsu interests, Aikawa, Asano, Furukawa, Iwazaki, Mitsui, Nakajima, Nomura, Okura, Sumitomo and Yasuda into national bonds inalienable for 10 years, Nov. 27.
The Holding Company Liquidation Commission designates twenty Japanese companies as holding companies, Dec. 3.
Miss Tamaki Uyemura, first Japanese civilian to visit the United States since Pearl Harbour received by President Truman, Dec. 5.

SCAP gives permission to the Japanese Government to sell surplus of the U.S. Forces subsistence stocks, consisting of $1,000,000 worth of medical apparatus, 1,200,000 pairs of socks, 100,000 trousers, 75,000 pounds of grease and 72,420 laundry soap, Dec. 16.
Large-scale demonstrative rallies against the Yoshida Cabinet staged in various parts of the Country. Dec. 17.
A great earthquake shakes Kinki, Shikoku and Kyushu districts, Dec. 21.
Japan's new school system established, Dec. 29.
Former Fleet Admiral Osami Nagano, who was Chief of the Naval General Staff during the Pacific War and one of the A-class war crimes suspects, dies of an acute form of pneumonia Jan. 5.
The SCAP issses an order prohibiting the general strike scheduled on February 1 of the Government and Public Workers' Union, Jan. 31.

The designation by the Holding Company Liquidation Committee of the 10 major zaibatsu, Mitsui, Iwasaki, Sumitomo, Yasuda, Asano, Okura, Nomura, Nakajima, Furukawa and Aikawa families, with their combined total securities of ¥1,165,000,000, Feb. 20.
The conversion rate of one American dollar military scrip to 50 yen announced, Mar. 11.
The conversion rates of military scrips of per one pound sterling, to ¥200, one Austrarian sterling to ¥160, and one rupee to ¥15 announced, Mar. 12.
In his letter addressed to Premier Yoshida General MacArthur calls attention to the Government's responsibility to adopt strong measures to readjust Japan's economic conditions, Mar. 22.
An Imperial rescript issued ordering the dissolution of the House of Representatives and the prorogation of the House of Peers, Mar. 31.
The House of Peers dissolved automatically with the abolition of peerage, Mar. 31.
The first public elections of prefectural governors, city mayors and village and town headmen held throughout Japan, Apr. 5.
SCAP gives permission to the Japanese Government for the reconstruction of Japanese rayon industry, Apr. 8.
The first post-surrender election of the members of the House of Councillors Apr. 20.
The Right Rev. Monseigeur Edward J. Flanagan, of Boys' Town, Nebrasak arrives in Tokyo, Apr. 23.
The general election of the members of the House of Representatives, Apr. 25.
The dissolution of the Privy Council and the Council of Princes of the Blood, Apr. 30.
For the first time the Emperor gives an interview to the press representatives, May 1.
Dr-Hitoshi Ashida appointed president of the Democratic Party, May 18.
The first session of the National Diet under the new Constitution opens, May 20.
Tetsu Katayama, President of the Social Democratic Party, nominated Prime minister by the Diet, May 23.
The Katayama Coalition Cabinet is formed, June 1.
SCAP authorizes the resumption of private international commercial relations with Japan as from August 15, June 10.
SCAP gives permission for Japanese whaling expeditions in the Antarctic waters, June 22.
The first session of the National Diet under the New Constitution is opened, June 22.

The Government announces the purge of those who cooperated with the military or propagated ultra-nationalistic ideas through newspapers, magazines, movies and radio and also Government officials who controlled the above functions during the period between July 7, 1936, when the China incident occurred, and December 7, 1941, when the Pacific War broke out. June 27.
The Government issues a “White Paper” to report on Japan's economic conditions, warning the nation of the serious situation in which she finds herself today, July 4.
The “lack Ship Festival” commemorating the visit of Commodore Perry to Japan held at Shimoda. The function is promoted for the first time since 1940, July 6.
The first gubernatorial conference sponsored by the Katayama Cabinet held at the Premier's official residence, July 6.
Rohan Kohda, member of the Imperial Academy and one of the most celebrated men of letters through the Meiji, Taisho and Showa eras, dies at his Ichikawa home, Chiba, at the age of 80, July 30.
Tadahiko Mibuchi, 67, former judge of the Supreme Court, recommended by the Katayama Cabinet as the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court under the new Constitution, July 31.
The four prefectures in the Tohoku district suffer the flood damages caused by the heavy rainfalls since July 21, Aug. 2.

A total of 576,344 purge cases were screened throughout the country during the seven-month period starting January 4 and ending on July 31 by the Central and Local Screening Committees. The Central Screening Committee handled 23,078 cases, of which 21,305 were cleared, 1077 disqualified for public offices and 66 cases left pending, Aug. 8.
The list of American and Canadian trade concerns permitted to participate in the forthcoming Japanese-American trade announced by SCAP, Aug. 10.
The reopening of Japan's foreign trade, Aug. 15.
A heavy flood works a havoc throughout Tokyo Metropolis and its 11 neighboring prefectures, Sept. 16.
The “Draper” Mission, headed by U.S. Undersecretary of the Army W. H. Draper arrives in Japan to study Japan's economic condition, Sept. 27.

The Imperial Household Council announces that fifty-one Imperial princes and princesses with the exception of three families of the Imperial brothers give up their Imperial ranks on October 14. The Imperial Household Economic Council grants them, with the exception of those engaged in active military service, the allowance of ¥47,475,000, Oct. 13.
The American President Lines ship General Gordon, 16,000 tons, enters Yokohama as the first civilian ship since the end of the War, Oct. 18.
Dr. Ikuo Oyama, noted pioneer organizer of labor movement in Japan returns to Japan from the United States after an absence of 16 years, Oct. 23.
A party of 11 delegates of the World's YWCA headed by Jonkvrouwe Cornelia M. van Asch van Wijick, former president of the association, arrives in Tokyo by airplane, Nov. 8.
Adoption of an interim currency arrangement by SCAP and the United Kingdom to facilitate private trade between sterling areas and Japan, Nov. 15.
The purge of all executive officers of Zaibatsu companies announced by the Government, Nov. 20.
The Government announce the purge of 81,225 regular and special volunteered army and navy officers and gendarmes and 167 high civil officials in the army and navy services, Nov. 28.
The Temporary Coal Mines Control Bill, is approved by the Diet, Dec. 8..
The central and local screening committees announce the purge cases totall 158,000, Dec. 10.
The Communist-controlled General Confederation of Labor orders 1,000,000 workers still on strike to return to work., Dec. 10.
The first general strike in 26 years of omnibus and streetcar transportation workers begins, Dec. 10.

parts.label: The World
rows: Greek chronology begins to be precise from this date.
Destruction of Nineveh. End of the Assyrian Empire.
Laws of the Twelve Tables published. The basis of all later Roman law.
Conquest of India by Alexander the Great.
Carthage and Corinth destroyed by the Romans.
Conquest of Gaul by Julius Cæsar.
Edict of Caracalla. Extended Roman citizenship to all free-born men in the Roman Empire.
Reorganization of the Roman Empire by Diocletian.
Edict of Milan. Granted general religious toleration and placed Christianity on a legal equality with the other religions of the Roman world.
Constantinople (New Rome) made the capital of the Roman Empire.
Deposition of Romulus Augustulus. Extinction of the line of Roman emperors in the West.
Codification of Roman law. One of the most important contributions of Rome to civilization.
The Sui Dynasty destroyed by the Tang Dynasty.
The flight of Mohammed from Mecca to Medina. Beginning of the Mohammedan era.
Defeat of Persia by the Saracens.
Supremacy of Silla among Korean kingdoms.
Conquest of Spain by the Saracens.
Leo III, Emperor of the East Roman Empire, publishes an edict for the prohibition of idolatry.
Battle of Tours. Stemmed the farther advance of the Moslems into western Europe.
Charlemagne crowned Emperor of the Romans. Formation of the so-called Holy Roman Empire.
Treaty of Verdun and 870 Treaty of Mersen. Marked important stages in the dissolution of Charemagne's dominions.
The Count of Paris installed by the French.
Alfred the Great divides England into three.
Attack of Constantinople by the Russians.
Otto I, the Great, crowned Roman Emperor. Revival of the Holy Roman Empire.
Christianity introduced into Russia. The Russian Slavs henceforth came under the influence of the Greek Church and Byzantine civilization.
Rupture of the Greek and Roman Churches. Destroyed the religious unity of European Christendom.
Battle of Hastings. Resulted in the Norman Conquest of England.
Council of Clermont. Beginning of the crusades.
Concordat of Worms. A compromise arrangement between the Papacy and the Holy Roman Empire.
Beginning of the Conquest of Ireland by the Englanders.
Conquests of Jenghis Khan. Brought a large part of western Asia and eastern Europe under Mongol sway.
Magna Carta. Defined the rights of Englishmen and inspired their later struggles for political liberty.
Travels of Marco Polo. His narratives greatly increased the interest of Europeans in the Far East.
Model Parliament of Edward I. A regularly elected Parliament which for the first time included representatives of all classes of the English people.
Osman I becomes ruler of the Ottoman Empire.
Black Death in Europe. Hastened the decline of serfdom and the emancipation of the peasantry.
The Great Schism. Weakened the spiritual supremacy of the Popes over western Christendom.
Greek first taught at Florence, Italy. The revival of Greek studies in western Europe formed an important aspect of the Renaissance movement.
Constantinople captured by the Ottoman Turks. End of the Byzantine Empire.
First book printed at Gutenberg's press in Mainz, Germany.
Cape of Good Hope rounded by Diaz.
India reached by Vasco da Gama. The Portuguese thus opened up an ocean passage from Europe round Africa to the Far East.
Luther's Ninety-five Theses posted. Beginning of the Protestant Reformation in Germany.
Publication of Copernicus' treatise “On the Revolutions of Celestial Orbits.”
Silver Mines of Potosi in Bolvia discovered. The enormous output of silver enlarged the supply of money in western Europe, thus stimulating industrial and commercial enterprises.
The Philippines taken by the Spanish.
The Union of Utrecht. Two years later the republic of the United Netherlands, or Holland took its place among European nations.
Defeat of the Spanish Armada gave England control of the sea and made possible English colonization of North America.
Edict of Nantes issued by Henry IV of France. A noteworthy step in the direction of religious toleration.
The British East India Company established.
Settlement of Jamestown. The first permanent English colony in America.
Authorized English Version of the Bible published.
The name “Manchuria” originated by a kingdom in that area.
Peace Treaty between Russia and Sweden.
Beginning of the Thirty Years' War.
Peace of Westphalia. Ended the religious wars.
Newton's “Principia” published. One of the most important contributions ever made to physical science.
The “Glorious Revolution.” Completed the work of the Puritan Revolution by overthrowing absolutism and divine right in England.
Battle of Blenheim. Defeated the attempt of Louis XIV to make France supreme in western Europe.
Rousseau's “Social Contract” published. Its democratic teachings were put into effect by the French revolutionists.
Peace of Paris. Ended the Seven Years War and gave to England a colonial empire in India and North America at the expense of France.
Voyages of Captain James Cook. Greatly increased geographical knowledge of the Pacific Ocean and its archipelagoes.
Arkwright's “water frame,” 1770 Hargreaves' “spinning jenny,” 1770 Crompton's “mule,” and 1785 Cartwright's power loom.
Declaration of Independence of the Americans.
Watt's steam engine patented. The steam engine invented in 1769 had served only for pumping; henceforth applied to manufacturing and transportation.
Constituion of the United States of America framed.
Meeting of the Estates-General in France. The first step toward the French Revolution.
Napoleon crowned Emperor of the French. The Code Napoleon promulgated. The most lasting memorial of the Napoleonic era.
Downfall of the Holy Roman Empire.
Fulton's steamboat, the “Clermont,” in successful operation.
Congress of Vienna. Remade the map of Europe after the revolutionary and Napoleonic era.
Battle of Waterloo. Brought about the final overthrow of Napoleon Bonarparte.
Stockton and Darlington Railway opened. The first line run by steam power.
The “July Revolution” in Europe. Overthrew absolutism and divine right in France and created modern Belgium.
Reform Act in Great Britain. The first step in democratizing the British government.
The Atlantic Ocean crossed by the “Great Western,” the first steamship to make the trip without using sails.
Texas annexed by the United States.
The “February Revolution” in Europe. Made France again a republic and led to revolutionary upheavals in Italy, Germany and the Austrian Empire.
Crystal Palace Exhibition at London. The first of the great international expositions.
The first submarine cable laid from Dover to Calais.
Occupation of Caucasia by the Russians.
Congress of Paris. Ended the Crimean War.
Canton occupied by the English and French forces.
Darwin's “Origin of Species” published. Presentation of the evolutionary theory.
The Peking Treaty. The English and French troops entered Peking.
Beginning of the Civil War in America.
Battle of Belgrade. Bismarck became Chancellor.
End of the American Civil War.
In 1866 Gladstone, leader of the House of Commons, introduced a measure for franchise reform, and the bill passed Parliament by the cooperation of Disraeli.
The Ausgleich. The constitution splitted the dominion of the Hapsburgs into two states, the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary.
Karl Marx's “Das Kapital” published. The first volume appeared in this year, but the second and third volumes were not published until after Marx's death.
Telephone invented by Alexander Graham Bell.
The Trade Union Act issued. Gave the British working classes the full right of organization.
Formation of the third Republic of France.
Queen Victoria assumes the title, Empress of India.
Tripartite Alliance among Germany, Austria and Italy.
Indo-China made a protectorate of France.
Rebellion of the Philippines against the Spanish government.
Invention of wireless telegraphy by Gogilielmo Marconi.
Spanish-American war. The Philippines made a territory of the United States.
Mukden in Manchuria occupied by the Russians.
Boycott of American goods by the Chinese.
Organization of the Union of South Africa.
Downfall of the Manchu Dynasty and birth of the Republic of China.
The Russian Revolution and establishment of Bolshevism in Russia.
First meeting of the League of Nations.
Italian Cabinet formed by Benito Mussolini.
Enforcement of the U.S. Federal Immigration Law. Practically prohibited the immigration of the Japanese into the United States.
Rise of anti-Japanese movement in China.
Around the world flight of the German airship “Zeppelin.”
Anti-British movement in India. Gandhi made prisoner.
Withdrawal of Germany from the League of Nations.
North Manchuria Railway transferred to Manchuria by the U.S.S.R.
Adolf Hitler made Fuhrer and Chancellor of Germany.
London naval conference of five Powers.
Anti-Comintern Agreement concluded between Germany and Japan.
Spanish Civil War spreads over the entire country.
Italy joins the Anti-Commintern Agreement, Nov. 6.
The Kuomintang Government removed to Chungking, Nov. 16.
The National Government of Spain founded by General Franco, Jan. 31.
The Anschluss of Austria proclaimed by Reichsfuhrer Hitler, Mar. 13.
The Renovation Government of the Republic of China founded under Wang Ching-wei at Nanking, Mar. 28.
British Prime Minister Chamberlain confers with the German Fuhrer.
Four-Power Conference at Munich, Sept. 30. Settled the Czech problem.
Anglo-Italian protocol becomes effective. Great Britain formally recognizes the Italian annexation of Abyssinia, Nov. 16.
Cultural agreement between Germany and Italy, Nov. 23.
Italy enters the London Treaty, Dec. 2.
Barcelona falls into the hands of the Franco forces, Jan. 26.
Franco Government of Spain recognized by Great Britain and France, Feb. 27.
Czech made a protectorate of Germany, Mar. 15.
Slovakia made a protectorate of Germany, Mar. 16.
Treaty of mutual assistance between Great Britain and Poland, Apr. 5.
Alliance of Germany and Italy, May 22.
Collision between German and Polish frontier guards reported, June 15.
Siam assumes a new national name “Thailand,” July 5.
Return of Danzig to Germany, July 21.
Non-aggression Pact between Germany and the U.S.S.R., Aug. 23.
Treaty of mutual assistance between Great Britain and Poland, Aug. 25.
Break of the Anglo-German negotiations on Polish issue, Aug. 31.
The European War, Great Britain and France declare war against Germany, Sept. 3.
Partition of Poland between Germany and the U.S.S.R., Sept. 18.
Annexation of Polish Corridor and Upper Silesia by Germany declared, Oct. 19.
British and French Governments reject the peace proposal of the Belgian King and the Queen of the Netherlands, November 7, Nov. 12.
Soviet Russia declares war against Finland, Nov. 29.
The League of Nations expels the U.S.S.R., Dec. 14.
President Roosevelt enunciates the non-involvement policy, Jan. 3.
Conclusion of the new commercial treaty between Germany and Russia, Feb. 12.
The Soviet Government announces the conclusion of the Peace Treaty with Finland, Mar. 13.
The Central Government of the Republic of China established at Nanking under Wang Ching-wei, Mar. 30.
Conclusion of the Commercial Treaty between Rumania and Germany, Apr. 20.
British Prime Minister Nevile Chamberelain resigns on May 10, and Winston Churchill forms the new War Cabinet on May 12.
German forces enter the Hague and the Dutch armies surrender, May 15.
German forces enter Brussels, while the Maginot Line is broken through by German forces at Sedan, May 17.
Italy's entry into the European War, June 10.
French army, surrenders to Germany, June 17.
Truce Agreement between Germany and France at Compiegne, June 22.
Truce between Italy and France, June 24.
Marshal Pétain assumes the position of the Head of France, July 12.
Chancellor Hitler proposes peace between Great Britain and Germany and Italy, July 19.
British Foreign Secretary Halifax rejects Hitler's proposal for peace, July 22.
German blitzkrieg intensifies over England, Aug. 10–27.
The Japan-Brazil cultural pact signed at Rio de Janeiro, Sept. 23.
President Roosevelt signs a proclamation prohibiting the export of scrap iron, steel and other iron materials to other than the western hemisphere and England, Sept. 26.
Chancellor Hitler and Premier Mussolini meet for the second time at the Brenner Pass, Oct. 4.
The U.S. State Department orders all Americans not engaged in pressing business in Japan, China, Manchuria French Indo-China and Hongkong to evacuate, Oct. 8.
President Roosevelt announces the American determination to fight the Tripartile Alliance, Oct. 12.
Beginning of the Greco-Italian war, Oct. 28.
President Roosevelt wins the presidential campaign over Wendell Willkie, Nov. 6.
Australia sends her first Minister, Sir John Greig Latham, to Tokyo, Dec. 20.
Henry Bergson, French philosopher, dies in Paris.
The American Congress passes the Lend-Lease Bill, Feb. 8.
Conclusion of the protocol between Thailand and French Indo-China concerning the settlement of the border dispute, Mar. 11.
German and Italian forces press British forces at the Libyan front, Apr. 13.
Greek forces surrender to German and Italian forces, Apr. 23.
Josef Stalin, Secretary General of the Central Committee of the Communist Party, concurrently appointed President of Council of People's Commissars, May 6.
Armistice between Great Britain and Iraq, May 31.
President Roosevelt issues order to freeze the assets of European countries held in the U.S., June 14.
Germany and Italy declare war against the U.S.S.R. June 22.
Great Britain and the U.S.S.R. come to an understanding concerning their mutual aid in their war against Germany, July 12.
The U.S.A. Government issues orders to “freeze” the Japanese assets held in that country, July 25.
The abrogation of the Commerce and Navigation Treaty between Great Britain and Japan of 1911 and the Commercial treaties between Japan and India and Burma of 1934 and 1937, July 26.
Dutch East Indies adopt similar economic measures with America concerning the transactions with Japan, July 28.
President Roosevelt and Premier Churchill meet on board the British Warship
The Atlantic Charter proclaimed on board the Prince of Wales off the Canadian on August 14.
The United States, Britain, Australia, Canada, the Netherlands East Indies, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Chungking and Cuba declare war on Japan, Dec. 8.
S.A. Lozovsky, Vice-Foreign Commissar of the U.S.S.R. reaffirms Soviet neutrality in relation to the Pacific War, Dec. 9.
Germany and Italy decide to wage war in concert with Japan against the United States and the British Empire, Dec. 11.
In Washington British Prime Minister Winston Churchill confers with President Roosevelt, Dec. 22.
The United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, Chungking, Canada and other Allied countries sign an agreement for no separate peace with the Axis Powers without mutual consultation, Jan. 2.
The Pan-American Foreign Ministers, Conference at Rio de Janeiro approves the severance of diplomatic relations with the Axis Powers, Jan. 23.
Benghazi, Libya, falls into the hands of German and Italian forces, Jan. 29.
An Allied Pacific Military Conference held in London, Feb. 10.
German forces commence offensive against Russia, bombarding Leningard, Mar. 15.
The British Government proposes to give a full dominion status to India after the conclusion of the War, Mar. 24.
Pierre Laval is installed the Premier of the French Government at Vichy, Apr. 14.
Chancellor Adolf Hitler and Premier Benito Mussolini hold conference, Apr. 29.
Madagascar attacked by British forces, May 5.
Powerful German forces commence attacks on South Russia, May 8.
The Alliance Treaty between Britain and Soviet Russia signed at London, May 26.
Tobruk, Libya occupied by German and Italian forces, June 21.
Matruh, Egypt reduced by German and Italian forces, June 29.
Gandhi and other leaders of India arrested, Aug. 8.
Brazil declares war on Germany and Italy, Aug. 22.
The French Government declares severance of diplomatic relations with the United States,. Nov 8.
The German forces advance into Toulon, Nov. 27.
The Vichy Government deprives Admiral Darlan and General Giraud of their French nationality, Nov. 27.
A German-Turkish pact signed in Berlin, Dec. 31.
The Nanking Government under Wang Ching-wei declares war on the United States and the British Empire, Jan. 9.
President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill consult for 10 days at Casablanca in French Morocco, Jan. 14–23.
Prime Minister Winston Churchill confers with Turkish President Ismet Inonu at Adana, Turkey, Jan. 30 and 31.
A conference between Chancellor Hitler and Premier Mussolini, Apr. 7–10.
The Executive Committee of the International Communist Party proposes the dissolution of the international organization, May 22.
Argentine revolution under the leadership of Pedro Ramirez, June 4.
Field-Marshall Archibald Wavell, Commander-in-Chief of the British force in India, appointed Viceroy and Governor-General of India, June 18.
The Soviet forces open offensive in the Smolensk area, July 1.
Powerful Anglo-American troops land on Sicily, July 10.
Chancellor Hitler confers with Premier Mussolini at Felt in Italy, July 19.
Rome raided by the American bomber plane units, July 19.
Premier Mussolini is suddenly forced to resign, and the Badoglio régime is established in Italy, July 25.
The second raid of Rome by American bombers, Aug. 13.
Sicily occupied by the Allied troops, Aug. 17.
The demise of King Boris III of Bulgaria, Aug. 28.
The landing of the British forces on a point of Italy proper opposite of Messina, Sept. 3.
An unconditional surrender of the Italian forces, Sept. 3.
A new Government created at the Northern Italy, Sept. 9.
The occupation of Rome by German forces, Sept. 10.
The rescue of Benito Mussolini by Adolf Hitler, Sept. 12.
Benito Mussolini declares the re-establishment of the Fascist Italy under his leadership, Sept. 15.
The Indecendence of the Philippines, Oct. 14.
Recognition by Germany and Burma of the new Republic of the Philippines, Oct. 16.
Conference held at Moscow among the U.S.A., Britain and the U.S.S.R., Oct. 19.
The Three-Power Foreign Ministers' Conference held at Moscow, Oct. 22.
The Bolivian Government headed by President Enrique Penaranda overthrown in coup d'état by the revolutionists, Dec. 20.
Count Galeazzo Ciano, former Italian Foreign Minister, and three other members of the defunct Fasscit Grand Council, executed in Verona, Jan. 11.
The United States Government freezes all bank accounts of Bolivians in America and also prohibit exports to Bolivia, Jan. 26.
Argentina's rupture of diplomatic relations with Japan, Jan. 27.
The granting of national defense and diplomatic autonomy to all the Soviet Republics by the Moscow Government, Feb. 3.
Brigadier-General Edelmiro Farrell formally assumes the post of President of Argentina as successor to General Pedro Ramirez on Mar. 10.
Recognition of the Badoglio régime of Italy by the Soviet Union, Mar. 13.
Colonel Frank Knox, United States Secretary of the Navy, dies, Apr. 28.
Powerful American forces land on Hollandia, New Guinea Island on May 27.
Evacuation of Rome ordered by the Fuehrer June 5.
The Anglo-American forces start landing operations at several points on the western coast of France, June 6.
King Victor Emanuele of Italy abdicates and relinquishes his position to Crown Prince Umberto. Marshal Pietro Badoglio tenders his resignation, June 6.
The severance of diplomatic relations between the U.S.A. and Finland, June 30.
General Charles de Gaulle's regime recognized by the U.S. government, July 11.
An attempt to assassinate Chancellor Adolf Hitler, July 19.
Manuel Quezon, President of the Philippines, dies at Saranac Lake, New York, Aug. 1.
The Anglo-American troops land at three places on the southern French coast, Aug. 15.
The Rumanian Cabinet under General Ion Antonescue resigns en bloc and King Michael orders an armistic with the Soviet Union, Aug. 23.
The Turkish government suspends diplomatic relations with the Petain government, Aug. 26.
German strongholds in Paris captured by the Anglo-American forces, Aug. 29.
Finland severing diplomatic relations with Germany, accepts the truce terms of the Soviet Union, Sept. 3.
The Soviet Union declares war on Bulgaria on Sept. 5.
British Prime Minister Winston Churchill confers with President Roosevelt at Quebec, Sept. 10.
Troops of the American 1st Army enter Luxemburg, Sept. 10.
The severance of Finnish-Japanese relations, Sept. 22.
Wendell Willkie, Republican leader of the United States, succumbs at the age of 52, Oct. 8.
The proclamation of independence of Annam, Mar. 11.
The Kingdom of Cambodia proclaims independence, Mar. 13.
The Kingdom of Luang-Prabang in Indo-China declares its independence, Apr. 8.
Koenisberg, capital of East Prussia captured by Soviet forces, Apr. 11.
Prisident Franklin D. Roosevelt succumbs unexpectedly at Warm Springs, Georgia. Harry S. Truman, Vice-President, sworn in as the new President, Apr. 12.
The United Nations Conference on International Security Organization in San Francisco opened, Apr. 25.
The formation of a provisional Austrian Government, headed by Dr. Karl Renner, Apr. 29.
Benito Mussolini and 12 members of the Fascist Cabinet executed by Italian partizans, Apr. 28.
Fuehrer Adolf Hitler commits suicide in Berlin, May 1.
Premier Stalin announces the complete occupation of Berlin, May 2.
Dr. Joseph Goebbels, German Minister for Propaganda and Public Enlightenment, commits suicide, May 2.
The Allied command formally announces the unconditional surrender of the German forces, May 7.
The German surrender terms ratified in Berlin, May 9.
The wartime coalition cabinet of Britain broken up with the resignation of Winston Churchill, May 23.
T.V. Soong made President of China's Executive Yuan, May 31.
The Big Four agreement on the control of Germany, June 5.
The San Francisco Conference completes the drafting of the Charter of the United Nations, June 23.
Marshal Josef Stalin is created “Generalissimo” of the Soviet Union, June 27.
James F. Byrnes appointed U. S. Secretary of State, July 2.
The U.S.A., British and Chinese governments recognize the Polish government of national unity, July 5.
The Italian government declares war on Japan, July 14.
The “Big Three” conference begins at Potsdam, July 16.
A joint declaration of the unconditional surrender of Japan issued by the U.S.A., Britain and China at Potsdam, July 25.
Clement Attlee, leader of the Labor Party, becomes Britain's new Prime Minister, July 27.
The Soviet Union declares war against Japan, Aug. 8.
The Soviet Army crosses the Manchurian frontier and commences offensive, Aug. 9.
Marshal Philippe Petain, former Chief of State of Vichy, sentenced to death on charge of treason, Aug. 16.
President Jose P. Laurel of the Republic of the Philippines issues a statement announcing the dissolution of the Republic, Aug. 17.
The Kurile Islands occupied by the Soviet Army, Sept. 1.
General Tomoyuki Yamashita, Commander-in-Chief of the Japanese Forces in the Philippines surrenders, Sept. 3.
The signing of the instruments of surrender concerning the territory of Korea south of 38 degrees North Latitude, Sept. 9.
The surrender of the Japanese forces in the Netherlands East Indies and in Borneo, Sept. 9.

The acceptance by Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten, Supreme Allied Commander of the Southeast Asia Command, of the surrender of the Japanese military and civilians in the territory of more than 1,500,000 square miles, Sept. 12.
The White House releases a 3,000 word text of “the initial post-surrender” policy for Japan, Sept. 22.
Pierre Laval, former Premier of the Vichy regime executed, Oct. 15.
General Charles de Caulle elected head of the provisional government of France, Nov. 13.
The immediate retirement of General George Marshall as Army Chief of Staff announced with the nomination of General Dwight Eisenhower as his successor, Nov. 20.
General George C. Marshall, former Chief of Staff appointed special envoy to China, Nov. 28.
The U.S.A. recognizes the new government of Yugoslavia headed by Marshal Joseph Tito, Dec. 22.
The Big-3 Foreign Ministers in Moscow agree to establish a four-power control council for Japan, Dec. 28.
A North Korean People's government established in the peninsula under the Soviet occupation by the Korean Communists, Feb. 19.
General Tomoyuki Yamashita, former Supreme Commander of the Japanese Forces to the Philippines, hanged to death at Los Banios, Feb. 23.
The U.S. War Department approves an interim plan for the revival of Japan's export trade, Mar. 18.
The Iranian Government files a formal protest with the UNO against the stationing of Soviet troops in Iran, Mar. 19.
Chen Kung-po, former President of the Nanking regime, given death sentence on charges of treason, Apr. 12.
Dr. Chu Min-yi, former Foreign Minister of the Nanking regime, given death sentence by the Kiangsu Supreme Court, and Mrs. Wang-Ching-wei the sentence of life-imprisonment, Apr. 22.
Manuel Roxas elected as President of the Philippine Commonwealth, May 28.
The United States extends $1,370 milion credit to France to help the French reconstruction program, May 28.
King Ananda Mahidol, 20, of Siam assassinated, June 9.
President Félix Couin resigns as head of the French Government, June 11.
Gerhardt Hauptmann, noted German playwright and 1912 winner of the Nobel prize, dies at 85, June 11.
A new French coalition government formed with Premier Georges Bidault, June 23.
President Manuel Roxas sworn in as president of the Republic of the Philippines, July 4.
The European Peace Conference opened at Luxembourg Palace, Paris. July 30.
H.G. Wells dies at the age of 79, Aug. 13.
The International Military Tribunal at Nurenberg decrees death by hanging for 12 former leaders of the Hitler regime, Oct. 2.
The ten A-class war criminals of Germany executed, Oct. 15.
Leo Blum, leader of the French Socialist Party elected premier of France, Dec. 12.
The Armed Services in Washington announce unification by President Truman of land, sea and air commands in which General MacArthur heads a Far East command, Dec. 17.
The exclusion of Japan and Germany from the International Olympic Games of 1948 announced, Dec. 24.
The promulgation of the Constitution of China, Jan. 2.
The United States makes a vigorous demand to Russia and China that the Manchurian port of Dairen be opened to the world under Chinese civil administration and free of Soviet military control, Jan. 7.
United States Secretary of State James Byrnes resigns and General of the Army George Marshall, appointed as his successor, Jan. 7.
France's Socialist Paul Ramadier forms a coalition cabinet with Georges Bidault of the Popular Republican Movement as foreign minister, Jan. 23.
The U.S. announcement of her withdrawal from the Triple Military Commission of China, Jan. 29.
The Peace Treaties between the five former Axis countries, Italy, Hungary, Rumania, Bulgaria and Finland, and the big four Allies and 17 other countries signed at Quai d'Orsay, Feb. 10.
Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek concurrently assumes the post of President of the Executive Yuan, following the resignation of Dr. T.V. Soong, Mar. 1.
Martial law imposed by the British in Jerusalem on 250,000 Jews in Palestine, Mar. 4.
A 50 year defense alliance between France and Britain to act jointly against any future aggression by Germany signed in Dunkerque, Mar. 5.
Martial law proclaimed all over Formosa by the Formosa Defense Commander against the so-called February 28 uprising started by Formosan Chinese under Communist instigation, Mar. 10.

The conclusion of the Japan-Philippines Trade Agreement through SCAP's good offices. As a result, the trade between the two countries will be settled directly in New York on dollar. The Philippine Republic will export 150 tons of hemp to Japan monthly, Mar. 17.
U.S. Secretary of State Marshall rejects Russia's bid for $10,000,000,000 worth of reparations from Germany, Mar. 19.
American Secretary of War Robert Patterson urges Congress to rush aid to Greece lest armed bands led by the Communists seize control, Mar. 25.
The signing of the Dutch-Indonesian Agreement recognizing the sovereignty of the Republic of Indonesia over Java, Sumatra and Madura, Mar. 25.
Death strikes down King George II of Greece, and his younger brother Prince Paul proclaimed successor, Apr. 1.
The United Nations Security Council approves an agreement giving the United States sole trusteeship over the vital strategic area of three Pacific island chains, Apr. 3.
The abdication of King Christian X of Denmark. The throne being succeeded by Crown Prince Frederick, Apr. 8.
General Chang Chun appointed Premier of China as successor to Dr. T.V. Soong, Apr- 17.
The Far Eastern Commission announces its policy of fixing the level of Japanese economy on a line of 1930-1934, Apr. 19.
The joint American-Soviet Conference on Korean problems, May 21.
British Prime Minister Attlee announces before the House of Commons the immediate transfer to India of the British sovereignty on India.
The United Nations Far Eastern Economic Conference held in Shanghai, attended by representatives of 10 nations, June 16.
The U.S. House of Representatives unanimously adopts a bill calling for permission for naturalization of the parents of the Nisei soldiers and sailors who were killed in the war, July 7.
European nations within the Soviet influence launched a concerted appeal to Moscow for sanction to participate in the Paris conference on Marshall's rehabilitation plan, July 9.
The engagement for Princess Elizabeth of England to Prjce Philip Mountbatten officially announced, July 10.

The Far Eastern Commission announces completion of the “basic post-surrender policy” for Japan which will make it possible to collect reparations from Japan in current and future production. The FEC policy, replaces the U.S. government's “initial post-surrender policy” issued in September 1945, July 10.
The European Rehabilitation Conference participated by 16 European nations excluding the Soviet-controlled nations held at Quai d'Orsai, July 12.
The Greek Government notifies the Security Council of the United Nations that a Communist-inspired guerilla force invaded Greece, July 15.
Former Premier of Burma U. Saw and 170 others arrested by the Rangoon police in connection with the assassination of Aung San and five other cabinet ministers, July 21.

Soviet Russia rejects the American invitation to an 11-nation preliminary conference on peace talk for Japan, and proposes instead the speedy con vocation of a four-power foreign ministers council, July 24.
The United Nations Security Council calls upon the Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia to cease hostilities immediately, Aug. 2.
The establishment of the new Dominion of India, Aug. 15.
The British Commonwealth Conference opened in Canberra with Minister for External Affairs Evatt as president, Aug. 26.
The United Nations Assembly elects Dr. Oswaldo Aranha of Brazil as its president, Sept. 16.

The European Economic Rehabilitation Conference adopts the plan that Western Europe pledge itself to a program of self help with the aid of $19,330,000,000 sent by the United States under a four year Marshall plan, Sept. 23.
The establishment of new Communist International organization announced in Moscow to fight the Marshall plan, Oct. 6.
The severance of diplomatic relation between Yugoslavia and Chile, Oct. 11.
The conclusion of the Anglo-Burmese Treaty providing for the complete independence of Burma in January 1948 in London, Oct. 17.
Gen. de Gaulle's Union of French People wins the election in Paris, securing 47 of the 90 municipal posts, of which the Communists obtain 27, Socialists 11 and the MRP five, Oct. 21.
Brazil breaks off diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union and Chile severes diplomatic relations with the USSR and also with Czechoslodakia, Oct. 22.
Premier Paul Ramadier of France forms a new cabinet composed of seven Socialists, three Popular Republicans, two Radical Socialists and one independent, Oct, 23.
The Royal wedding ceremony of Princess Elizabeth Alexandra Mary of Britain and Lt. Philip Mountbatten is held at Westminster Abbey, Nov. 20.
Stanley Baldwin, three times British Prime Minister, passes away at his home at the age of 80, Dec. 13.
U.S. and great Britain sign new German occupation pact, Dec. 18.

President Truman signs the bill providing $18,000,000 for China, $522,000,000 for Western Europe in emergency stop-gap aid, and $340,000,000 for army occupation costs in Korea, Japan, Austria and Germany, Dec. 24.
Former King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy succumbs at Alexandria Hospital, Egypt, of pneumonia, at the age of 78, Dec. 28.
King Michael I of Rumania abdicates and a republican government is established in Rumania, Dec. 30.

former general, commander of Special Service Section in Manchuria, chief adviser to the North China autonomous government and Inspector General of Military Training.

commander of an artillery regiment at the Rape of Nanking and of Japanese forces which shelled the Ladybird and the Panay, a founder of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association and alleged to have been a promoter of plots to remove politicians not considered sufficiently aggressive.
former Field Marshal, member of Supreme War Council, War Minister and Commander-in-Chief of the Expeditionary Force in Central China from July 1940 to 1944.
Prime Minister in 1939, former president of the Privy Council and cabinet minister under Konoye.
Prime Minister from March 1936 to February 1937, and Foreign Minister under Saito, Okada and Konoye.
chief of General Affairs in Manchoukuo in July 1937, president of the Planning Board under Konoye and Chief Secretary and Minister of State under Tojo.
former general, Chief of Staff of Kwantung Army and War Minister under Konoye and Hiranuma.
Minister of Finance under Konoye in 1937 and 1938, president of the North China Development Company and Minister of Finance under Tojo.
Cabinet minister under Konoye and Hiranuma, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal from 1940 to 1945, chief confidential adviser to the Emperor and chairman of meetings of ex-premiers.
former general, Chief of Staff of the Kwantung Army, Vice-War Minister under Konoye and Tojo and Commander-in-Chief of the Japanese Army in Burma in 1944.
former general, Prime Minister from July, 1944 to April, 1945, Chief of Staff of the Kwantung Army, Overseas Minister under Hiranuma dnd Yonai and Governor-General of Korea in 1942.

former general, Commander-in-Chief of Japanese Forces in Central China in 1937 and 1938, member of the Cabinet Advisory Council in 1938 and 1939 and president of the Greater East Asia Development Society.

Foreign Minister under Konoye in 1940 and 1941, chief delegate to the League of Nations Assembly in 1933, and president of the South Manchuria Railway from 1935 to 1939 (died on June 7, 1946 and his indictment dismissed accordingly).
former general, member of the Privy Council from 1942 to 1945, War Minister in 1931 and Commander-in-Chief of Kwantung Army from 1934 to 1936.
Former lieutenant general and Chief of the Military Affairs Bureau of the War Ministry from 1939 to 1942 and chief of Staff of the 14th Area Army in the Philippines under Yamashita in 1944.

former admiral, Navy Minister under Hirota, Commander-in-Chief of the Combined Fleet in 1937 and member of the Supreme War Council in 1940 (died on January 5, 1947, and accordingly his indictment dismissed).

an officer of the South Manchuria Railway alleged to have been an organizer of the Mukden Incident on September 18th, 1931 and a propagandist for the expulsion of the white races from Asia by aggressive war (on account of his mental condition the Tribunal removed him from the trial, April 9, 1947).
former vice-admiral, chief of the Military Affairs Bureau of the Navy from 1940 to 1944 and Vice-Navy Minister under Koiso in 1944.
ambassador to Germany 1938 and 1939 and from 1941 to 1945.
former lieutenant general, Chief of the Military Affairs Bureau of the War Minister from 1942 to 1944.
Foreign Minister under Tojo and Koiso from April 1943 to April 1945, and former Ambassador to U.S.S.R., Great Britain and "National Government" of Nanking.
former admiral, Navy Ministry under Tojo in 1941 and member of Supreme War Council in 1944.
Ambassador to Italy in 1939 and adviser to the Japanese Foreign Office in 1940.
president of the Cabinet Planning Board and Minister without Portfolio under Konoye and Tojo from 1941 to 1943.
Foreign Minister under Tojo from October 1941 to March 1942 and under Suzuki in 1945.
former general, Premier and War Minister from December 2nd, 1941 to July, 1944.
former general, Vice-War Minister from 1936 to 1938, commander of the Kwantung Army from 1939 to 1944 and Chief of the General Staff in 1944 and 1945.
